insight: newApp target uses PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup: .swift files and subfolders compile automatically with no pbxproj edit, and ANY other file left in newApp/newApp/ ships as a bundle resource. Bundling fonts = drop .otf in the tree + register UIAppFonts in Info.plist, no pbxproj work.

With GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE=YES and INFOPLIST_FILE both set, an INFOPLIST_KEY_* build setting WINS over the same key written into Info.plist. Portrait lock required editing INFOPLIST_KEY_UISupportedInterfaceOrientations in project.pbxproj; adding UISupportedInterfaceOrientations to Info.plist alone had no effect. CFBundleDisplayName in Info.plist did work (no competing build setting).

To derive a design system from a reference screenshot, sample it programmatically rather than by eye: Counter over region crops for flat fills, and a brightest-pixel-by-saturation pass for antialiased text colours. Eyeballing understates text hues by 20-30% value.

With PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup, resources are copied FLAT into the bundle root regardless of on-disk folder. UIAppFonts entries must therefore be bare filenames; a path like Resources/Fonts/X.ttf registers nothing and SwiftUI .custom() silently falls back to the system face with no warning or log. Assert UIFont.fontNames(forFamilyName:) in a debug self-check.

Text("\(someInt) XP") goes through LocalizedStringKey and applies a number formatter, so 2340 renders as "2 340". In monospaced readouts this breaks alignment. Use Text(verbatim:) for any numeral in a mono context.

Display serifs like Instrument Serif carry a generous line box; a Text with a 104pt glyph lays out roughly 2x the glyph height. Constrain with .frame(height: size * 0.86) or the containing card doubles in height.
